why: Found while auditing for MISSING labels (v80). Neither list was acted on: removals need their own pass with their own rules (docs/plans.md §1), and a downgraded claim is not evidence of a wrong existing label. Every `wrong_labels` entry was checked to be present in the corpus at the time of writing.

wrong_labels.label: divide-and-conquer-dp
wrong_labels.why: that is monotone opt; this is a cartesian-tree dp

wrong_labels.label: dsu-on-tree
wrong_labels.why: plain Kruskal DSU, no small-to-large merging

wrong_labels.label: centroid-decomposition
wrong_labels.why: rerooting dp; the statement merely says centroid

wrong_labels.label: stack
wrong_labels.why: needs a max-heap; LIFO gives a wrong answer

wrong_labels.label: rolling-hash
wrong_labels.why: a hash set of visited segments

downgraded_claims.label: binary-lifting
downgraded_claims.why: True as one implementation: doubling the cell->cell map ~20 times gives each cell's eventual position. But it is a device for 'iterate the map many times', and the corpus already carries cycle-detection/SCC, which is the alternative implementation of the same step. The structural fact the corpus is missing is that this is a functional graph.

downgraded_claims.label: coordinate-compression
downgraded_claims.why: Factually fine (verified h_i, x <= 1e9 on the real statement), but compression is only what lets you index a value-keyed segment tree; a dynamic/implicit segment tree over 0..1e9 removes it entirely. The actual missing label is the value-indexed segment tree with a descend-to-find-the-level query — the corpus has neither segment-tree nor any data-structure label here.

downgraded_claims.label: euler-tour
downgraded_claims.why: True — tin/tout on the suffix-link tree is how 'visited states below the terminal node' becomes one BIT range sum. But it is the standard companion of Aho-Corasick counting rather than the idea; aho-corasick (the other claim on this row) is the label that actually fixes this entry.

downgraded_claims.label: euler-tour
downgraded_claims.why: The mechanism is described correctly, but the Euler tour is the last step of the real construction: reverse the deletions to build the Kruskal reconstruction tree, at which point a component is a subtree. The corpus has kruskal-reconstruction-tree in the taxonomy with ZERO problems using it — that is the label this problem is missing.

downgraded_claims.label: euler-tour
downgraded_claims.why: Accurate, but the tour is used only for an ancestor predicate (is x between the originating vertex and the DSU top boss at that time), never for a range query. The taxonomy has a label that names exactly this use, and it is already applied to 9 problems.

downgraded_claims.label: fenwick-tree
downgraded_claims.why: The BIT is genuinely needed (sliding window over j, threshold on pref[i]+suf[j]), but all the difficulty is the reduction: z-functions on both sides plus turning the overlap condition into a window on j-i. The aggregation is interchangeable machinery, and the corpus's real hole here is the string label — it says kmp and string-hashing, not z-function.

downgraded_claims.label: heap
downgraded_claims.why: True — the accepted greedy runs several priority queues of candidate deltas (add a_i, upgrade b_i-a_i, swap b_j-a_i, downgrade). But the heaps are how the regret/exchange greedy is implemented; the idea is the exchange argument that every added star takes the cheapest reversible move. A heap searcher lands on a 2600 greedy where the container teaches them nothing.

downgraded_claims.label: heap
downgraded_claims.why: The container is incidental — a multiset works identically; what makes the algorithm correct and fast is the small-to-large merge plus the 'pop the deepest, re-add at this depth' greedy. The other claim on this problem names that properly.

downgraded_claims.label: lca
downgraded_claims.why: The up/down difference counters split at the LCA are described correctly, but they are the second half of the solution — the problem's identity is bridges plus the bridge tree (inside a 2-edge-connected component any orientation works). Adding lca while the corpus has no bridge label at all fixes the smaller gap; note bridge-tree and bridges are canonical but carry ZERO problems today.

downgraded_claims.label: monotonic-stack
downgraded_claims.why: True: the leftward chain-reaction reach is a next-greater-style stack sweep, and a second stack carries the right-push candidates. But it is supporting machinery inside a 2700 prefix DP; someone searching monotonic-stack to learn or drill the pattern gets no return here.

downgraded_claims.label: offline-queries
downgraded_claims.why: The problem has no queries. It asks for a single count of pairs (x,y); sorting the sweep order is just a sweep, not reordering user queries to answer them out of order. I checked the corpus's 59 offline-queries problems and every one has an actual query list (Tree and Queries, Bipartite Checking, Zip-line...), so this would be the odd one out and would dilute the label.

downgraded_claims.label: ordered-set
downgraded_claims.why: Factually fine (n <= 1000 so O(n^2 log n) is comfortable), but the insight is that the first removed pair must contain the global maximum, so you brute-force the partner. The multiset is a replaceable container — sorting descending with a pointer plus a value->count hash map does the same job without an ordered structure.

downgraded_claims.label: partition-dp
downgraded_claims.why: No piece-count dimension and no cut enumeration anywhere in the accepted solution - it is dp[i][0/1] 'extend or start here' in O(n), which is a linear state machine that happens to describe a split. A partition-dp searcher wants dp[i][j] over cut points and would learn nothing here.

downgraded_claims.label: prefix-sum
downgraded_claims.why: The idea is the harmonic sweep over (y, multiple k) with the check 'does any element lie in [k*y, k*y+y-1]'; prefix sums over the value-count array are one line of scaffolding under it. A prefix-sum searcher would get a number-theory counting problem where prefix sums are incidental.

downgraded_claims.label: segment-tree
downgraded_claims.why: True but one ingredient of three at 3400: the crux is the divide-and-conquer decomposition of the free area into O(n log^2 n) rectangles (already carried), on top of which the segment-tree edge compression is the standard follow-through. Least representative segment-tree problem in this batch for anyone searching the term.

downgraded_claims.label: segment-tree
downgraded_claims.why: This is a segment tree over the time axis - a divide-and-conquer recursion skeleton for offline dynamic connectivity - not a range-query structure, and the idea is already named by dsu-rollback + offline-queries. Someone searching 'segment tree' would be looking for the other kind.

downgraded_claims.label: stack
downgraded_claims.why: The algorithm is greedy counting over v = 0..n; the stack of spare duplicates is a container choice that works only because v is scanned in increasing order - a sorted pool or a pointer does the same job. True, but not what a 'stack' searcher is practising.

downgraded_claims.label: subtree-dp
downgraded_claims.why: One DFS aggregating (red, blue) counts per subtree, then a local test per edge - correct, but this is subtree counting rather than a DP, and dfs is already carried. Harmless, marginal; the interesting label here would be whatever names the two-sided colour condition, and the taxonomy has none.
